questions.q: In the 7-step variational loop described in the lesson, which single step is the only one that touches the QPU?
options: Step 3: executing the circuit for N shots and returning measurement counts
Step 1: initializing the parameters
Step 5: the optimizer proposing new parameters
Step 6: checking the convergence criterion
questions.explain: Only circuit execution (step 3) runs on quantum hardware. Initialization, cost computation, the optimizer step, convergence checking, and returning the result are all classical.

questions.q: Using the parameter-shift rule on a circuit with 10 parameters, how many circuit evaluations does ONE iteration require?
options: 21 (10 params x 2 shifts + 1 for the cost evaluation itself)
10 (one evaluation per parameter)
2 (one up-shift and one down-shift, regardless of parameter count)
100 (10 params squared)
questions.explain: The parameter-shift rule needs 2 evaluations per parameter (shifted up and down) plus 1 evaluation for the cost function itself: (10 x 2) + 1 = 21.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a gradient-free optimizer like SPSA can be cheaper per iteration than a parameter-shift gradient method, even though it's often noisier?
options: SPSA needs only 2 circuit evaluations per iteration regardless of how many parameters the circuit has, while parameter-shift needs 2 evaluations PER PARAMETER
SPSA doesn't require any circuit evaluations at all
SPSA only works on classical simulators, so it never incurs hardware cost
SPSA always converges in fewer total iterations than parameter-shift methods
questions.explain: SPSA's per-iteration cost (2 evaluations) doesn't scale with parameter count, unlike parameter-shift (2 x params). This can make it far cheaper per iteration for circuits with many parameters, at the cost of noisier gradient estimates.

questions.q: The lesson computes a full 150-iteration, 8-parameter VQE run on real IonQ Aria hardware at about $77,265. What is this number primarily meant to demonstrate?
options: Why development and debugging of the loop logic happens against a free/near-free classical simulator, with real hardware reserved for a much smaller number of confirmatory runs
That variational algorithms are never worth running on real hardware under any circumstances
That AWS Braket's per-shot pricing is a mistake that will be corrected
That 8-parameter circuits are too large for any current QPU to execute
questions.explain: The huge cost of running every development iteration on real hardware is exactly why classical simulators are used to verify optimizer, cost-function, and convergence logic first -- real hardware is reserved for final, smaller-scale confirmatory runs.

questions.q: If the $77,265 full-150-iteration run in the lesson instead converges and stops at iteration 60, what is the approximate cost, and what classical mechanism made that saving possible?
options: About $30,906; the convergence criterion stopped the loop early once improvement in the cost function flattened out
Still $77,265; convergence checks don't affect QPU spend
About $77,265 / 8, because cost scales with parameter count, not iteration count
$0; converging at iteration 60 means no circuits were ever submitted
questions.explain: Cost scales linearly with the number of iterations actually run (60/150 x $77,265 ~= $30,906). The convergence criterion -- a classical tolerance or plateau check -- is what stops the loop before it burns through all 150 iterations' worth of QPU calls.
